\chapter{Chapter08 — Biased Threshold Complements}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from FABL.Chapter08.BiasedThresholdComplements
\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{FABL.Chapter08.BiasedThresholdComplements}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Prefix of a permuted path]
\lean{FABL.maximalPathPrefix}
\label{FABL.maximalPathPrefix}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\pi$ be a permutation of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and let
$k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$. The maximal path prefix at $k$ is the set of indices
$i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ for which $\pi(i)<k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Size of a permutation path prefix]
\lean{FABL.card_maximalPathPrefix}
\label{FABL.card_maximalPathPrefix}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.maximalPathPrefix}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $\pi$ be a permutation of $[n]$, and let $k$ be an
integer with $0\le k\le n$. The set of indices $i$ for which the value $\pi(i)$ is less
than $k$ has cardinality $k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Distribution of maximal path prefixes]
\lean{FABL.maximalPathLayerPMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p239-b009}
\label{FABL.maximalPathLayerPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.maximalPathPrefix}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $0\le k\le n$. Choose a permutation of
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ uniformly at random, and take its maximal path prefix at level $k$.
The resulting probability mass function is the distribution of that prefix as a finite
subset of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Uniform maximal path point distribution]
\lean{FABL.uniformMaximalPathPointPMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p239-b009}
\label{FABL.uniformMaximalPathPointPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.maximalPathLayerPMF}
Let $n$ be a natural number. Choose a level uniformly from $\{0,\ldots,n\}$, then sample
a finite subset according to the maximal path prefix distribution at that level. The
resulting probability mass function is the distribution of the sampled subset.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Uniformity from constant point masses]
\lean{FABL.pmf_eq_uniformOfFinset_of_constant_on}
\label{FABL.pmf_eq_uniformOfFinset_of_constant_on}
\leanok
\difficulty{5}
Let $\alpha$ be a finite type, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\alpha$, and
let $S\subseteq\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set. Suppose $p(a)=0$ for every $a\notin S$,
and $p$ takes the same value at every pair of elements of $S$. Then $p$ is the uniform
probability mass function on $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Permutation transporting equal-cardinality subsets]
\lean{FABL.finsetTransportPerm}
\label{FABL.finsetTransportPerm}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of the $n$ indices with
equal cardinality. The transport permutation is the permutation obtained by extending a
bijection from $A$ to $B$ to the full set of indices.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Membership under a finite-set transport]
\lean{FABL.mem_finsetTransportPerm_iff}
\label{FABL.mem_finsetTransportPerm_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.finsetTransportPerm}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $A,B\text{Fin}(n)$ be finite sets of equal
cardinality. For the permutation of $\text{Fin}(n)$ that transports $A$ onto $B$, an
index $i\text{Fin}(n)$ is mapped into $B$ exactly when it belongs to $A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Permutation transport of a prefix set]
\lean{FABL.maximalPathPrefix_mul_transport_eq_iff}
\label{FABL.maximalPathPrefix_mul_transport_eq_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.finsetTransportPerm, FABL.maximalPathPrefix, FABL.mem_finsetTransportPerm_iff}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ with
equal cardinality. For any $k$ from $0$ through $n$ and any permutation $\pi$ of
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, the set of indices whose images under $\pi$ composed with the
inverse of the permutation transporting $A$ to $B$ are less than $k$ equals $B$ if and
only if the set of indices whose images under $\pi$ are less than $k$ equals $A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Equal probabilities for equal-sized sets]
\lean{FABL.maximalPathLayerPMF_eq_of_card_eq}
\label{FABL.maximalPathLayerPMF_eq_of_card_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.finsetTransportPerm, FABL.maximalPathLayerPMF, FABL.maximalPathPrefix, FABL.maximalPathPrefix_mul_transport_eq_iff}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $k$ be an integer from $0$ through $n$, and let
$A,B\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ have the same cardinality. Under the distribution
obtained by choosing a uniformly random permutation and taking the set of elements whose
images are less than $k$, the probability of obtaining $A$ equals the probability of
obtaining $B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform distribution on a subset layer]
\lean{FABL.maximalPathLayerPMF_eq_uniformLayer}
\label{FABL.maximalPathLayerPMF_eq_uniformLayer}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.card_maximalPathPrefix, FABL.maximalPathLayerPMF, FABL.maximalPathLayerPMF_eq_of_card_eq, FABL.pmf_eq_uniformOfFinset_of_constant_on, FABL.powersetCard_univ_nonempty}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $k$ be an integer from $0$ through $n$. Choosing a
uniformly random permutation of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ and taking the elements whose images
are less than $k$ gives the uniform distribution on the $k$-element subsets of
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p075-b002}
\proofstep
  {FABL.restrictSubsetTo_liftSubsetFrom}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p075-b002}
\proofstep
  {FABL.card_liftSubsetFrom}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p075-b002}
For every natural number $n$, choose a permutation of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ uniformly at
random and independently choose $k$ uniformly from $\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$. The set of the
first $k$ elements in the permutation has the same probability distribution as first
choosing $k$ uniformly from that range and then choosing a $k$-element subset of
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$ uniformly at random.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Restriction of a subset to an index set]
\lean{FABL.restrictSubsetTo}
\label{FABL.restrictSubsetTo}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $J$ and $S$ be subsets of the $n$ indices. The
restriction of $S$ to $J$ consists of the elements of $J$ that also belong to $S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Lifting a subset from an index set]
\lean{FABL.liftSubsetFrom}
\label{FABL.liftSubsetFrom}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ be a subset of the $n$ indices, and let $T$ be a
subset of $J$. Its lift to the full index set is the subset of the $n$ indices
consisting of the underlying indices of the elements of $T$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Restriction after lifting a subset]
\lean{FABL.restrictSubsetTo_liftSubsetFrom}
\label{FABL.restrictSubsetTo_liftSubsetFrom}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.liftSubsetFrom, FABL.restrictSubsetTo}
\difficulty{3}
Let $J$ be a finite set of coordinates and let $T$ be a subset of $J$. If $T$ is viewed
as a subset of the ambient coordinate set and then restricted back to $J$, the result is
$T$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Lifted subset lies in its indexing set]
\lean{FABL.liftSubsetFrom_subset}
\label{FABL.liftSubsetFrom_subset}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.liftSubsetFrom}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ be a finite subset of $\mathbin n$, and let $T$ be a
finite subset of the elements of $J$. Viewing the elements of $T$ as elements of $\mathbin n$
gives a subset contained in $J$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cardinality of a lifted subset]
\lean{FABL.card_liftSubsetFrom}
\label{FABL.card_liftSubsetFrom}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.liftSubsetFrom}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ be a finite subset of a set of $n$ coordinates, and
let $T$ be a finite subset of $J$. The image of $T$ in the full coordinate set has the
same cardinality as $T$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Restriction of a union with a disjoint subset]
\lean{FABL.restrictSubsetTo_union_compl}
\label{FABL.restrictSubsetTo_union_compl}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.liftSubsetFrom, FABL.restrictSubsetTo}
\difficulty{5}
Let $J$ be a finite set of coordinates, let $T\subseteq J$, and let $U$ be a finite set
of ambient coordinates contained in the complement of $J$. Then restricting the union of
the ambient copy of $T$ with $U$ back to $J$ gives $T$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Restriction and set difference decomposition]
\lean{FABL.lift_restrict_union_sdiff}
\label{FABL.lift_restrict_union_sdiff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.liftSubsetFrom, FABL.restrictSubsetTo}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $J,S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ be finite sets. The
elements of $S$ that lie in $J$, lifted back to the ambient set, together with the
elements of $S$ outside $J$, form exactly $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Disjointness from a complementary subset]
\lean{FABL.disjoint_liftSubsetFrom_of_subset_compl}
\label{FABL.disjoint_liftSubsetFrom_of_subset_compl}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.liftSubsetFrom, FABL.liftSubsetFrom_subset}
\difficulty{4}
Let $J$ and $U$ be subsets of the coordinate set $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and let $T$ be a
set of coordinates belonging to $J$. If $U$ is contained in the complement of $J$, then
the image of $T$ in the full coordinate set is disjoint from $U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Shapley layer weights on complementary subsets]
\lean{FABL.sum_shapleyLayerWeight_add_card_compl}
\label{FABL.sum_shapleyLayerWeight_add_card_compl}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integral_bernoulliSubsetMass_eq_shapleyLayerWeight, FABL.shapleyLayerWeight}
\difficulty{6}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $t$ be a
natural number with $t\le |J|$. Using the layer weight $w(n,k)=1/((n+1)\binom{n}{k})$,
the sum of $w(n,t+|U|)$ over all subsets $U$ of the complement of $J$ equals $w(|J|,t)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Shapley subset distribution on a fixed set]
\lean{FABL.shapleySubsetPMFOn}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p240-b002}
\label{FABL.shapleySubsetPMFOn}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.shapleySubsetPMF}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $J$ be a subset of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. Transfer the
Shapley subset distribution on a set of size $|J|$ to the subsets of $J$ using the
canonical relabeling between $J$ and $\{0,\ldots,|J|-1\}$. The resulting probability
mass function is a distribution on the finite subsets of $J$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Shapley subset marginal distribution]
\lean{FABL.shapleySubsetMarginalPMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p240-b002}
\label{FABL.shapleySubsetMarginalPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.restrictSubsetTo, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $J$ be a subset of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. Sample a
subset according to the Shapley subset distribution on $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ and restrict
it to $J$. The resulting probability mass function is the distribution of that
restricted subset.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Pushforward mass under an equivalence]
\lean{FABL.pmf_map_equiv_apply}
\label{FABL.pmf_map_equiv_apply}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be finite types, let $p$ be a probability mass function on
$\alpha$, let $e:\alpha\to\beta$ be a bijection, and let $b\in\beta$. The mass at $b$ of
the probability mass function obtained by transporting $p$ along $e$ equals
$p(e^{-1}(b))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Probability of a subset of a finite set]
\lean{FABL.shapleySubsetPMFOn_apply_toReal}
\label{FABL.shapleySubsetPMFOn_apply_toReal}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmf_map_equiv_apply, FABL.shapleyLayerWeight, FABL.shapleySubsetPMFOn, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply_toReal_eq_layerWeight}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $J$ be a subset of $\text{Fin}(n)$, and let $T$ be
a subset of $J$. Under the Shapley subset distribution on subsets of $J$, the
probability of selecting $T$ is $1/((|J|+1)\binom{|J|}{|T|})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Difference after adjoining a disjoint set]
\lean{FABL.sdiff_lift_union_compl}
\label{FABL.sdiff_lift_union_compl}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.liftSubsetFrom, FABL.liftSubsetFrom_subset}
\difficulty{4}
Let $J$ be a subset of a finite coordinate set, let $T$ be a subset of $J$, and let $U$
be a subset of the complement of $J$. Then the set difference between the union of $T$
and $U$ and $J$ is exactly $U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Marginal subset probability]
\lean{FABL.shapleySubsetMarginalPMF_apply_toReal}
\label{FABL.shapleySubsetMarginalPMF_apply_toReal}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.card_liftSubsetFrom, FABL.disjoint_liftSubsetFrom_of_subset_compl, FABL.liftSubsetFrom, FABL.lift_restrict_union_sdiff, FABL.restrictSubsetTo, FABL.restrictSubsetTo_union_compl, FABL.sdiff_lift_union_compl, FABL.shapleyLayerWeight, FABL.shapleySubsetMarginalPMF, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF_apply_toReal_eq_layerWeight, FABL.sum_shapleyLayerWeight_add_card_compl}
\difficulty{6}
Let $J$ be a subset of an $n$-element set and let $T$ be a subset of $J$. Under the
distribution obtained by restricting a Shapley-random subset to $J$, the probability of
obtaining $T$ is $1/((|J|+1)\binom{|J|}{|T|})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Marginal distribution on a subset]
\lean{FABL.shapleySubsetMarginalPMF_eq_shapleySubsetPMFOn}
\label{FABL.shapleySubsetMarginalPMF_eq_shapleySubsetPMFOn}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.shapleySubsetMarginalPMF, FABL.shapleySubsetMarginalPMF_apply_toReal, FABL.shapleySubsetPMFOn, FABL.shapleySubsetPMFOn_apply_toReal}
\difficulty{3}
Let $J$ be a subset of an $n$-element set. The distribution obtained by restricting a
Shapley-random subset to $J$ equals the Shapley subset distribution on a ground set of
size $|J|$, with elements identified through the order-preserving enumeration of $J$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Reindexed marginal distribution]
\lean{FABL.shapleySubsetMarginal_reindex_eq}
\label{FABL.shapleySubsetMarginal_reindex_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmf_map_equiv_apply, FABL.shapleySubsetMarginalPMF, FABL.shapleySubsetMarginalPMF_eq_shapleySubsetPMFOn, FABL.shapleySubsetPMF, FABL.shapleySubsetPMFOn}
\difficulty{4}
Let $J$ be a subset of an $n$-element set. After identifying $J$ with a set of $|J|$
elements by its enumeration, the restriction to $J$ of a Shapley-random subset has the
Shapley subset distribution on that $|J|$-element set.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Refined threshold level]
\lean{FABL.refinedThresholdLevel}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b009}
\label{FABL.refinedThresholdLevel}
\leanok
For a real number $\tau$, define the refined threshold level to be $\tau/(1+\tau)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Refined threshold constant]
\lean{FABL.refinedThresholdConstant}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b009}
\label{FABL.refinedThresholdConstant}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.refinedThresholdLevel}
For a real number $\tau$, define the refined threshold constant to be
$4\bigl(\tau/(1+\tau)\bigr)^{1-\tau}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Refined threshold cutoff]
\lean{FABL.refinedThresholdCutoff}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p238-b009}
\label{FABL.refinedThresholdCutoff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.refinedThresholdConstant}
For real numbers $\tau$, $\epsilon$, and $p_c$, let $C(\tau)$ denote the refined
threshold constant at $\tau$. Define the refined threshold cutoff to be
$C(\tau)\,\epsilon^{1+\tau}p_c$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Range of the refined threshold level]
\lean{FABL.refinedThresholdLevel_mem_Ioo}
\label{FABL.refinedThresholdLevel_mem_Ioo}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.refinedThresholdLevel}
\difficulty{3}
For every $\tau\in(0,1)$, the refined threshold level $\tau/(1+\tau)$ lies strictly
between $0$ and $1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Complement of the refined threshold level]
\lean{FABL.one_sub_refinedThresholdLevel}
\label{FABL.one_sub_refinedThresholdLevel}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.refinedThresholdLevel}
\difficulty{3}
For every real number $\tau>0$, the refined threshold level satisfies
$1-\mathrm{refinedThresholdLevel}(\tau)=\frac{1}{1+\tau}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Refined lower logarithmic ratio]
\lean{FABL.refinedLowerLogRatio}
\label{FABL.refinedLowerLogRatio}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$, and let $r,p\in\mathbb R$.
Define the refined lower logarithmic ratio by $\log q_f(p)-(1-r)\log p$, where $q_f(p)$
is the polynomial biased probability that $f$ outputs $-1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity of the refined logarithmic ratio]
\lean{FABL.refinedLowerLogRatio_monotoneOn}
\label{FABL.refinedLowerLogRatio_monotoneOn}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.biasSigma, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_mem_Ioo, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.continuous_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.deriv_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_ge_logistic, FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq_totalInfluence, FABL.productTotalInfluence, FABL.refinedLowerLogRatio, FABL.strictMonoOn_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\difficulty{6}
Let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function on the sign cube, and let
$r,p_a\in(0,1)$. If the biased minus-probability polynomial of $f$ at $p_a$ is at most
$r$, then the refined logarithmic ratio, as a function of $p$, is nondecreasing on
$(0,p_a]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Refined power bound]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_le_refined_rpow}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_le_refined_rpow}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_mem_Ioo, FABL.refinedLowerLogRatio, FABL.refinedLowerLogRatio_monotoneOn}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function
on the $n$-dimensional sign cube. Suppose $0<r<1$, $0<p\le p_a<1$, and the biased-minus
probability polynomial of $f$ at $p_a$ is at most $r$. Then its value at $p$ is at most
$r(p/p_a)^{1-r}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Refined small-parameter bound]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_le_epsilon_refined}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_le_epsilon_refined}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_endpoints, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_le_epsilon_of_le_sq_mul_critical, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_le_refined_rpow, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_mem_Ioo, FABL.one_sub_refinedThresholdLevel, FABL.refinedThresholdConstant, FABL.refinedThresholdCutoff, FABL.refinedThresholdLevel, FABL.refinedThresholdLevel_mem_Ioo}
\difficulty{6}
Let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube.
Suppose $\tau\in(0,1)$, $\epsilon\in(0,\tau/(1+\tau))$, $p_c\in(0,1/2)$, $p\ge0$, the
biased minus-probability polynomial at $p_c$ equals $1/2$, and
$p\le4(\tau/(1+\tau))^{1-\tau}\epsilon^{1+\tau}p_c$. Then the polynomial at $p$ is at
most $\epsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Endpoint lower bound for the logarithmic derivative]
\lean{FABL.deriv_neg_log_one_sub_probability_ge_endpoint}
\label{FABL.deriv_neg_log_one_sub_probability_ge_endpoint}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.biasSigma, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_mem_Ioo, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.deriv_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_ge_logistic, FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq_totalInfluence, FABL.productTotalInfluence, FABL.strictMonoOn_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\difficulty{5}
Let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be monotone and nonconstant. For each $S\subseteq[n]$,
let $\widehat f(S)$ be its Fourier coefficient under the uniform measure, and define
$q_f(t)=\bigl(1-\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}(1-2t)^{|S|}\widehat f(S)\bigr)/2$. If
$p_c,p\in(0,1)$, $p_c\le p$, and $q_f(p_c)=1/2$, then
$\left.\frac{d}{dt}\bigl[-\log(1-q_f(t))\bigr]\right|_{t=p}\ge \frac{1}{2(1-p)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Endpoint threshold logarithmic ratio]
\lean{FABL.endpointThresholdLogRatio}
\label{FABL.endpointThresholdLogRatio}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$, and let $p\in\mathbb R$.
Define the endpoint threshold logarithmic ratio by $-\log(1-q_f(p))+\tfrac12\log(1-p)$,
where $q_f(p)$ is the polynomial biased probability that $f$ outputs $-1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity of the endpoint threshold log ratio]
\lean{FABL.endpointThresholdLogRatio_monotoneOn}
\label{FABL.endpointThresholdLogRatio_monotoneOn}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.biasSigma, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_mem_Ioo, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.continuous_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.deriv_neg_log_one_sub_probability_ge_endpoint, FABL.endpointThresholdLogRatio, FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq_totalInfluence, FABL.productTotalInfluence}
\difficulty{6}
Let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function on a finite sign cube, and let
$p_c,b\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<p_c<\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac12\le b<1$. If the biased-minus
probability polynomial of $f$ has value $\tfrac12$ at $p_c$, then the function $p\mapsto
-\log(1-B_f(p))+\tfrac12\log(1-p)$ is monotone on $[\tfrac12,b]$, where $B_f$ denotes
that polynomial.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Lower bound near the upper endpoint]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_one_sub_ge_one_sub_sqrt}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p239-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p239-b001
}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_one_sub_ge_one_sub_sqrt}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_mem_Ioo, FABL.endpointThresholdLogRatio, FABL.endpointThresholdLogRatio_monotoneOn, FABL.strictMonoOn_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function
on the $n$-dimensional sign cube. Suppose $0<p_c<1/2$, $0<\delta<1/2$, and the
biased-minus probability polynomial of $f$ at $p_c$ equals $1/2$. Then
$1-\sqrt{\delta/2}$ is at most the value of that polynomial at $1-\delta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Composed majority split cube]
\lean{FABL.ComposedMajoritySplitCube}
\label{FABL.ComposedMajoritySplitCube}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign}
For a natural number $m$, the composed majority split cube is the set of pairs
consisting of a sign assignment on two coordinates and a sign assignment on $2m+1$
coordinates.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Majority of three values]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeValue}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p043-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p118-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p118-b007
}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeValue}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.majority}
For $a,b,c\in\{1,-1\}$, define their majority value to be the element of $\{1,-1\}$ that
occurs at least twice among $a,b,c$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Composed majority split]
\lean{FABL.composedMajoritySplit}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p044-b007,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p239-b004
}
\label{FABL.composedMajoritySplit}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.ComposedMajoritySplitCube, FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeValue}
For a natural number $m$, define the composed majority map on pairs of sign assignments,
one on two coordinates and one on $2m+1$ coordinates, by first taking the majority of
the latter assignment and then taking the three-input majority of that sign together
with the two signs in the first assignment.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Composed majority split equivalence]
\lean{FABL.composedMajoritySplitEquiv}
\label{FABL.composedMajoritySplitEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.ComposedMajoritySplitCube, FABL.Sign}
For a natural number $m$, the set of sign assignments on $2+(2m+1)$ coordinates is
equivalent to the product of the set of sign assignments on two coordinates and the set
of sign assignments on $2m+1$ coordinates, by splitting the coordinates into these two
blocks.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Composed majority on a Boolean cube]
\lean{FABL.composedMajority}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p044-b007,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p239-b004
}
\label{FABL.composedMajority}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.composedMajoritySplit, FABL.composedMajoritySplitEquiv}
For a natural number $m$, identify the $2+(2m+1)$ coordinates of the Boolean cube with
two signs and a block of $2m+1$ signs. The composed majority function applies majority
to the block and then takes three-input majority of that output and the two remaining
signs.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity of three-sign majority]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeValue_monotone}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeValue_monotone}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majority_monotone}
\difficulty{1}
Order the signs by $-1<1$ and order triples coordinatewise. The function that returns
$1$ when the sum of the three signs is nonnegative and returns $-1$ otherwise is
monotone: if one triple is coordinatewise at most another, its output is at most the
other's output.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p044-b007}
\proofstep
  {FABL.majorityThreeValue}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p021-b001,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p044-b007}
\proofstep
  {FABL.composedMajoritySplit}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p044-b007}
\proofstep
  {FABL.composedMajoritySplitEquiv}

  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p044-b007}
\proofstep
  {FABL.composedMajority}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p044-b007}
For every natural number $m$, the composed majority function on sign vectors of length
$2+(2m+1)$ is monotone: if one input vector is at most another coordinatewise in the
order $-1<1$, then its output sign is at most the other output sign.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Composed majority is nonconstant]
\lean{FABL.composedMajority_isNonconstant}
\label{FABL.composedMajority_isNonconstant}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.composedMajority, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeValue, FABL.majority_unanimous}
\difficulty{4}
For every integer $m\ge 0$, the composed majority on the sign cube of dimension
$2+(2m+1)$ is nonconstant: it takes different values on at least two inputs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Three-input majority indicator identity]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeValue_neg_indicator}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeValue_neg_indicator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeValue, FABL.thresholdSign}
\difficulty{4}
For signs $a,b,c\in\{-1,1\}$, the indicator that their three-input majority is $-1$
equals the sum of the three pairwise products of the indicators that each sign is $-1$,
minus twice the product of all three indicators.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased split-cube probability distribution]
\lean{FABL.composedMajoritySplitPMF}
\label{FABL.composedMajoritySplitPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.ComposedMajoritySplitCube, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
Let $m$ be a natural number and let $p\in[0,1]$. On pairs of sign assignments, take the
product distribution in which each sign in both blocks is drawn independently from the
biased sign distribution with parameter $p$: the first block has two coordinates and the
second has $2m+1$ coordinates.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Mass of the split majority distribution]
\lean{FABL.composedMajoritySplitPMF_apply}
\label{FABL.composedMajoritySplitPMF_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.ComposedMajoritySplitCube, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.composedMajoritySplitPMF, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
\difficulty{5}
Let $m\ge 0$, let $p\in[0,1]$, and let $h$ be a pair consisting of two signs and $t$ a
tuple of $2m+1$ signs. Under the distribution obtained by independently sampling the two
coordinates of $h$ and the coordinates of $t$ from the sign law that assigns probability
$p$ to $+1$ and $1-p$ to $-1$, the probability mass of $(h,t)$ is the product of the
probability mass of $h$ and the probability mass of $t$ under their respective product
distributions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Product law under a split-coordinate equivalence]
\lean{FABL.productProbabilityPMF_map_composedMajoritySplitEquiv}
\label{FABL.productProbabilityPMF_map_composedMajoritySplitEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.composedMajoritySplitEquiv, FABL.composedMajoritySplitPMF, FABL.composedMajoritySplitPMF_apply, FABL.pmf_map_equiv_apply, FABL.productProbabilityPMF, FABL.productProbabilityPMF_apply}
\difficulty{4}
Let $m$ be a natural number, and let $p\in[0,1]$. The image of the product distribution
of $2+(2m+1)$ independent samples from the biased sign distribution with parameter $p$,
under the equivalence that splits the coordinates into blocks of sizes $2$ and $2m+1$,
is the distribution obtained by first sampling the two blocks independently from their
respective product distributions and then pairing them.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Negative-output probability]
\lean{FABL.composedMajoritySplitProbability}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p239-b005}
\label{FABL.composedMajoritySplitProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.composedMajoritySplit, FABL.composedMajoritySplitPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation}
Let $m$ be a natural number and let $pef{in}$ the interval $[0,1]$. Under the
probability mass function on split-cube inputs specified by $m$ and $p$, the
composed-majority split probability is the probability that the output sign is $-1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Split and cube minus probabilities agree]
\lean{FABL.composedMajoritySplitProbability_eq_biasedMinusProbability}
\label{FABL.composedMajoritySplitProbability_eq_biasedMinusProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasedMinusProbability, FABL.composedMajority, FABL.composedMajoritySplitProbability, FABL.pmfExpectation_map, FABL.productMean, FABL.productProbabilityPMF_map_composedMajoritySplitEquiv}
\difficulty{3}
Let $m\ge 0$ and $p\in[0,1]$. The probability that the split composed majority of
independent biased signs (each sign is $+1$ with probability $p$ and $-1$ with
probability $1-p$) equals $-1$ is equal to the probability that the composed majority on
the full sign cube equals $-1$ under the same independent biased-sign law.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Negative-sign probability]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF_negIndicator}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF_negIndicator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF}
\difficulty{2}
Let $0<p<1$, and choose a sign $X\in\{-1,1\}$ according to the probability distribution
with mean $1-2p$. The expected value of the indicator of the event $X=-1$ is $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of a biased sign indicator]
\lean{FABL.productMean_headIndicator}
\label{FABL.productMean_headIndicator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF_negIndicator, FABL.pmfExpectation_const_one, FABL.pmfExpectation_independentProductPMF_prod, FABL.productMean, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
\difficulty{4}
Let $0<p<1$ and choose one of two coordinates, $i\in\{0,1\}$. For two independent signs,
each equal to $-1$ with probability $p$, the mean of the indicator that the sign in
coordinate $i$ is $-1$ is $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of a product of sign indicators]
\lean{FABL.productMean_headIndicator_mul}
\label{FABL.productMean_headIndicator_mul}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF_negIndicator, FABL.pmfExpectation_independentProductPMF_prod, FABL.productMean, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
\difficulty{3}
Let $0<p<1$. For two independent signs, each equal to $-1$ with probability $p$, the
mean of the product of the indicators that each sign is $-1$ is $p^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Composed majority probability formula]
\lean{FABL.composedMajority_probability_formula}
\label{FABL.composedMajority_probability_formula}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.composedMajority, FABL.composedMajoritySplit, FABL.composedMajoritySplitPMF, FABL.composedMajoritySplitProbability, FABL.composedMajoritySplitProbability_eq_biasedMinusProbability, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeValue_neg_indicator, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_add_fun, FABL.pmfExpectation_bind, FABL.pmfExpectation_const, FABL.pmfExpectation_map, FABL.pmfExpectation_smul_fun, FABL.pmfExpectation_sub_general, FABL.productMean_headIndicator, FABL.productMean_headIndicator_mul, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
\difficulty{5}
For every natural number $m$ and every real $p$ with $0<p<1$, the biased
minus-probability polynomial of the composed majority on $2+(2m+1)$ coordinates
satisfies
\[
P_{\mathrm{comp}}(p)=p^2+2p(1-p)P_{\mathrm{maj}}(p),
\]
where $P_{\mathrm{comp}}$ denotes that polynomial for the composed majority and
$P_{\mathrm{maj}}$ denotes it for majority on $2m+1$ coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Fixed-bias majority error bound]
\lean{FABL.fixedBiasMajorityError}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p239-b004}
\label{FABL.fixedBiasMajorityError}
\leanok
For a real number $d$ and a natural number $m$, the fixed-bias majority error is
$2\exp(-4d^2m)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Decay of fixed-bias majority error]
\lean{FABL.tendsto_fixedBiasMajorityError_zero}
\label{FABL.tendsto_fixedBiasMajorityError_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fixedBiasMajorityError}
\difficulty{3}
For every real $d>0$, the function of natural numbers given by $m\mapsto 2\exp(-4d^2m)$
converges to $0$ as $m\to\infty$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Biased Majority Error Below Half]
\lean{FABL.tendsto_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_majority_odd_of_lt_half}
\label{FABL.tendsto_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_majority_odd_of_lt_half}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasedMinusProbability, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_mem_Ioo, FABL.biasedMinusProbability_majority_lower_le_two_mul_exp, FABL.fixedBiasMajorityError, FABL.majority, FABL.majority_monotone, FABL.majority_odd_isNonconstant, FABL.tendsto_fixedBiasMajorityError_zero}
\difficulty{5}
Fix $p\in(0,1/2)$. For each odd number $2m+1$ of independent signs, with each sign equal
to $-1$ with probability $p$, the probability that their majority is $-1$ tends to $0$
as $m\to\infty$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Biased Majority Error Above Half]
\lean{FABL.tendsto_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_majority_odd_of_half_lt}
\label{FABL.tendsto_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_majority_odd_of_half_lt}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasedMinusProbability, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_mem_Ioo, FABL.fixedBiasMajorityError, FABL.majority, FABL.majority_monotone, FABL.majority_odd_isNonconstant, FABL.one_sub_two_mul_exp_le_biasedMinusProbability_majority_upper, FABL.tendsto_fixedBiasMajorityError_zero}
\difficulty{5}
Fix $p\in(1/2,1)$. For each odd number $2m+1$ of independent signs, with each sign equal
to $-1$ with probability $p$, the probability that their majority is $-1$ tends to $1$
as $m\to\infty$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Composed majority disagreement limit]
\lean{FABL.tendsto_composedMajority_probability_of_lt_half}
\label{FABL.tendsto_composedMajority_probability_of_lt_half}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.composedMajority, FABL.composedMajority_probability_formula, FABL.majority, FABL.tendsto_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_majority_odd_of_lt_half}
\difficulty{4}
For every $p$ with $0<p<\tfrac12$, the biased minus-probability polynomial of the
composed majority on $2+(2m+1)$ coordinates converges to $p^2$ as $m\to\infty$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Composed Majority Error Above Half]
\lean{FABL.tendsto_composedMajority_probability_of_half_lt}
\label{FABL.tendsto_composedMajority_probability_of_half_lt}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.composedMajority, FABL.composedMajority_probability_formula, FABL.majority, FABL.tendsto_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_majority_odd_of_half_lt}
\difficulty{4}
Fix $p\in(1/2,1)$. For each $m$, take two independent signs and an independent block of
$2m+1$ signs, all with probability $p$ of being $-1$. First take the majority sign of
the block, then take the majority of that sign and the two initial signs. The
probability that the resulting sign is $-1$ tends, as $m\to\infty$, to $1-(1-p)^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Composed majority at unbiased input]
\lean{FABL.composedMajority_probability_one_half}
\label{FABL.composedMajority_probability_one_half}

\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $m$, the biased minus-probability polynomial of the composed
majority on $2+(2m+1)$ coordinates, evaluated at $p=1/2$, equals $1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Critical probability of composed majority]
\lean{FABL.criticalProbability_composedMajority}
\label{FABL.criticalProbability_composedMajority}

\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $m$, the critical probability of the Boolean function obtained
by splitting an input of length $2+(2m+1)$ into blocks of lengths $2$ and $2m+1$, taking

first block, is $\frac12$.
\end{theorem}
